paragraphs: Conjunctions
Now you know the basics about writing simple sentences. If you earned an A on your first assignment, you may begin putting these simple sentences together into longer, compound sentences.
A compound sentences consists of two simple sentences or clauses joined by a conjunction.
The conjunction is a connecting word that joins two clauses or two complete sentences.
You already know many of these words and use them everyday.
There are three types of conjunctions. These are:
3. Correlative.
2. Subordinating.
1. Coordinating.
Remember that conjunctions not only “connect” two words, clauses, or sentences, but also express a precise relationship between those words, clauses, or sentences.
Coordinating conjunctions join sentence parts that are the same.
There are seven of these. They are:
for, and, nor, but, or, yet, and so.
For example:
I studied all weekend and am ready for the exam.
Ping wanted to visit his parents, but he missed his flight home.
The professor felt sorry for us so she gave us another week to prepare our presentation.
Correlative conjunctions work just like coordinating conjunctions, but they always work in pairs. Examples include:
Either … or           neither … nor
both … and           not only … but also
whether … or.
For example:
Either you are for the reforms or you are against them.
Both faculty and administration recommend a longer semester.
The courts not only struck down the new law, but also made clear that any similar laws would be invalidated.

Subordinating conjunctions are a little bit trickier. They connect an independent clause (complete sentence) to a dependent clause (often not a complete sentence). They may also connect adverb clauses to an independent clause.
Examples include: after, because, if, since, unless, and when.
We will watch a movie after we eat dinner.
We will quit early if everyone is finished.
The charity will close unless it obtains new funding.
You improved your writing because you used the writing process.
We must book tickets before the airline sells out.
As you write these longer sentences, keep in mind that while many conjunctions may be a grammatical “fit,” there is usually only one conjunction that expresses your precise meaning!
SO take the time to make certain you use the right conjunction!
And don’t forget everything else you have learned about S/V/O, S/V agreement, passive verb phrases, and so forth!
We look forward to reading your next essay!
